title: The windhover
hook: a falcon hanging on the wind stirs a priest's hidden heart, and readers still argue over one word (The Windhover)
tomorrow: a little girl is crying over falling leaves. what's she crying for?

segments.voice: Yesterday, dappled things: the trout and the freckle giving glory just by being themselves, from a beauty past change. Today, Hopkins looks up, and something up there gets to him.

A skater lands the jump clean. A carpenter splits a board with one stroke. Even strangers cheer for mastery like that. Hopkins found it in a bird. Out early, he watches a falcon hang on the wind, ride it, then swing off in one smooth arc. And he writes: "My heart in hiding / Stirred for a bird, – the achieve of, the mastery of the thing!" Why hiding? He told a friend that when he became a Jesuit, he burned the poems he'd written and resolved to write no more unless his superiors wished it. Above this one he wrote: To Christ our Lord.
screen: `MASTERY, LANDED CLEAN.` → `A FALCON RIDING THE WIND.` → `MY HEART IN HIDING STIRRED.` → `TO CHRIST OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Then comes a word readers still argue over: "Buckle!" Readers split, and both sides are serious Christian readings. One side hears buckle as clasp together. All the bird's beauty, valor and pride buckle into one, and a fire breaks out, a billion times lovelier, and the poet cries, O my chevalier, my knight. On this reading the falcon is a picture of Christ in glory, the way the dedication suggests. The other side hears buckle as give way, the way a beam buckles under weight. The proud flight breaks, and something lovelier comes out of the breaking. Look at how the poem ends. A plow's plain work, "sheer plod makes plough down sillion / Shine", and dull embers that fall, break open, and gash gold-vermilion. On this reading the hidden heart is the point. In Christian teaching, Christ's glory is the cross, power given away. Paul writes that Christ "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant". Theologians call that self-emptying kenosis. So one reading says the falcon shows who Christ is. The other says the plodding priest does, the one who burned his poems and kept walking behind the plow. Hopkins never settles it. He stirs for the bird, and he dedicates the poem to Christ, who took the form of a servant.
screen: `BUCKLE: CLASPED TOGETHER?` · `BUCKLE: GIVING WAY?` · `PLOW AND EMBERS: SHINE IN THE PLOD.` · `KENOSIS: THE FORM OF A SERVANT.` · then, large: `MY HEART IN HIDING.`

segments.voice: Step to a window, or outside, and find one thing riding the wind: a bird, a leaf, a flag, a strand of cloud. Watch it for two minutes without naming anything. If something in you stirs, let it, and don't hurry to explain it.
The windhover: an old country name for a kestrel, the small falcon that hangs in place on the wind. In Hopkins's poem, it wakes a hidden heart.
Keep this: my heart in hiding, stirred for a bird and offered to Christ. Day done.

fork.reveal: after Buckle! the poem turns to sheer plod and to embers that fall and gash gold-vermilion. that ending is the strongest evidence for the giving-way reading, and the clasping reading still has the dedication and the chevalier.
